note: The Democrat of 1835-07-15, Vol. II No. 13, read through — and it is the worst text in the corpus. The deposit holds ONE transcription of this issue, a `-2` OCR rebuild whose own QA note records a median cross-pass agreement of four per cent, so it is a SOLE WITNESS at the weakest tier: there is nothing to check it against and its own transcribers did not trust it. The reading is made accordingly. Seven claims are made where the type is legible enough to carry one, every uncertain reading stays inside `[uncertain: …]` or square brackets in `normalized`, and NO PERSON IS MINTED OUT OF A CROP-EDGE NAME — the Chicago Reading Room's committee (c001) and the secretary who signed its resolutions are left unminted for exactly that reason, as are the letter lists at c007. The issue's one substantial find is c001: the board of the Chicago Reading Room resolving to seek a two-thousand-dollar joint-stock building ON THE PUBLIC SQUARE, containing the reading room and usable as a meeting or lecture room. It is a building PROPOSED and not a building standing, and the claim says so. NO CHICAGO POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST: swept for every form the Democrat uses, for three hits, all of them the Hennepin, Plainfield and Du Page returns of 1 July 1835 reprinted from the previous week.

[At] a m[ee]ting of the [board] of [dire]ctors of the […] Chicago [R]eading Roo[m], he[ld] at the […] [uncertain: Tremont] H[ou]se on Monday evening, July [uncertain: 13th], [for the] purpose of consulting upon [ways and mean]s f[o]r obtaining a bu[il]ding suitable for [th]e [Re]ading Roo[m], the follow[in]g preamble [and] re[s]o[luti]ons were adopted, viz: Whereas it ha[s] been suggested that a [j]o[in]t stock company might be [formed] in Chicago, that [w]ould appropriate [about] $2[,000] for a building con[taining] […] [a] Reading Room, [and] as [it] […] [m]i[ght] be used for a meeting [or] lecture room, and [for] other public pur[poses]; [an]d [it is understood] that [a site] can [uncertain: be obtained] for a company to place [the propo]sed […] building on the Public Square […] [st]reet; a[n]d belie[ving] that such a b[ui]lding [would] be a great convenience to [the] Reading Roo[m] Assoc[iation] as well as to the pub[l]ic generally; while its p[ro]prietor[s] may be enabled, [by] the rents [at] reasonable rates […] [it is] ther[e]fore fully approv[ed …] […] Resolved, That C. Petit[…] [and …] H. Moore, be app[o]i[n]te[d] a comm[ittee …] to take [su]ch further steps as may be ne[cessary …] on the part of this boar[d] with regard to the contem[p]lated build[ing] […] that these resolutions be pu[blished in] the newspapers of this place. […] Secretary[.] [Chic]ago, July 1[3], 1835
claims.notes: A BUILDING PROPOSED, NOT A BUILDING STANDING, and the distinction is the whole of what may be taken from this claim. The board of directors of the Chicago Reading Room met, and resolved to seek a joint stock company that would appropriate about two thousand dollars for a building containing the Reading Room and usable as a meeting or lecture room, on the understanding that a site could be had ON THE PUBLIC SQUARE. Nothing here says such a building was ever put up, and nothing in the model may stand on it. WHY NO PERSON IS MINTED: this issue is the `-2` OCR rebuild, the weakest tier in the corpus, and the two committee names arrive as 'C. Petit' and 'Beae H Moore' with the secretary's signature reduced to 'a Hra@ity Mucus' — the ticket's own instruction is not to mint a person out of that, so none is minted. WHAT IS UNCERTAIN AND MARKED AS SUCH: the house the board met in reads 'the oy Cal Treacot Uhese', which is a Tremont House to the eye and is left inside `[uncertain: …]` rather than asserted; the meeting date reads 'July font' and is read as the Monday of that week, 13 July 1835, also marked. THE SUM AND THE SITE ARE THE LEGIBLE PART and are why the claim is made: '$2.' for '$2,000' is a crop of a printed figure, and 'buidiag on the Public Syware' is not ambiguous. The Public Square is already in the model, and a reading room proposed for it in the scene month is a fact about the square in July 1835 whether or not the building followed.

claims.notes: THE EAGLE COFFEE HOUSE, NAMED AS THE TOWN'S MEETING PLACE, and that is why this notice is worth a card. The same house is the anchor of the only relative placement in the four issues — Cooley and Halsman's tailoring shop stands on Dearborn Street 'nearly opposite the Eagle House' (chicago_democrat_1835_07_22 c006) — so the two claims corroborate each other: a coffee house prominent enough to hold a precinct meeting and to serve as a street anchor. NOT A PLACEMENT ITSELF: this notice gives the Eagle Coffee House no street, and none is inferred here. The notice is reprinted in the 1835-07-22 issue (page 3 column 2, lines 313-317), whose text is the poorer of the two; this printing is the witness. No person is minted — the notice is signed only 'By order of the Committee'.

And […] said el[e]ction to be con[du]cted […] [I have hereunt]o set my hand and […] the [s]eal of State to be a[ffixed at] Vandalia, the […] Sheriff [of Cook County,] hereby give[s] notice to all th[e judges] of the Elections [in] all [the] precinct[s] in said county, t[o] hold a[n] [el]ection and open [th]e[ir] poll books for the [election in] place of J[a]mes W. claims.notes: AN ELECTION ORDERED INTO THE TOWN IN THE SCENE MONTH: a state senate seat covering La Salle, Putnam and Cook fell vacant on James W. Stephenson's resignation, the Governor issued his writ to the Sheriff of Cook County, and Silas W. Sherman gave notice that the judges of election in every precinct in the county were to open their poll books on the first Monday of August. That is a public event in Chicago on 3 August 1835, five weeks after the scene date, and the officers it names are county officers who were in place before it. THE TEXT IS THE WORST IN THE RANGE and the normalized reading is bracketed heavily to say so — twenty-five short crop-edge lines woven with a neighbouring column, in the rebuild the ticket rates the weakest tier of this corpus. TWO NAMES ARE MINTED AND NO MORE: 'Jeweph Nanean' is Joseph Duncan, who signs the State Bank proclamation in the next issue over a legible signature (chicago_democrat_1835_07_22 c008), and 'HILAS W. SHERMAN, Shan' is Silas W. Sherman, sheriff — both are read from office as much as from type, and the reasoning is written here rather than assumed. 'Jainea W. Ss' is NOT minted: the senator's surname is cut and Stephenson is a supposition, so it stays inside brackets in the normalized reading and mints nobody.

claims.notes: THE HOUR, AND WHY THIS PRINTING IS RECORDED AT ALL. Three witnesses in this range carry the Land Office notice and they do not agree on when the office opened: this one reads 'af 10° clo A.M.', the 1835-07-29 printing reads the same ten o'clock, and the 1835-07-08 deposit printing — the best text of the three — reads nine. Two against one, and the odd one out is the best witness, so nothing is settled and all three readings are on the record (see chicago_democrat_1835_07_08 c003). THE DATELINE is taken from the 07-08 printing's legible 'o. July 3, 1835.—4w12', which is the same insertion with the same four-week order; the verbatim here is the sheared form, as the schema requires it to be.

claims.notes: A REPRINT, RECORDED AND NOT MINTED — and the reprint is the finding. These are the SAME three out-of-county returns of 1 July 1835 the 1835-07-08 issue printed (chicago_democrat_1835_07_08 c018-c020), standing a second week, over the same three postmasters' names. Under T-0299 one list makes one cohort of people however many times it is printed, so nothing is minted here on either ground: they are not Chicago lists, and they are not new. WHY THIS WITNESS IS WORTH QUOTING ANYWAY: the segmenter cut the 07-08 deposit printing down the middle and sheared the left alphabetical column's surnames off, while this rebuild delivers the whole block on one line with BOTH columns present ('Atwater, Theinae 2 Kee, Walla na Allen, Archibold Leonard, Bi'). The two witnesses are complementary — one is legible and half, the other is whole and mangled — and neither on its own is a list a person may be minted from. That is the reading, and it is why the 1 July 1835 Hennepin list is left unminted in this epic until a better witness turns up. The lists are reprinted a third time on 1835-07-22 (page 4, line 425).
